parts.title: Activities for different needs
parts.instructions: Match each person to a suitable option. Some options are extra.
parts.passage:
A. Park Walkers
Join a Sunday morning walk in a park. The guide teaches newcomers how to follow trail signs. All activities are outdoors and no experience is needed.

B. Wildlife Watch
Help university researchers count butterflies on Tuesday afternoons. You need to recognize several familiar species. Bring a notebook to record your observations.

C. Study Reset
Spend twenty minutes in the school library on Friday at lunch. Try a short breathing exercise and talk about how to switch off your phone before studying. No change of clothes is needed.

D. Paddle Club
Practice kayaking on Wednesday evenings. All boats and safety equipment are included. This session is for people who have already done a beginner course.

E. Bike Repair
An indoor weekend class about fixing simple bike problems. You do not have to bring a bike to the workshop.

F. Balcony Garden
Grow herbs at home with a beginner group. The class meets on Wednesday mornings and provides all seeds.

parts.title: A different kind of lunch break
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose one answer for each question.
parts.passage:
For most of the school year, I ate lunch at my desk so I could start my homework before the afternoon classes. I felt pleased when I got an exercise done early, but I often lost concentration in my last lesson. My friend Ana usually went outside. One day she asked me to join her, and I decided to test her routine for a week.

At first, leaving my work behind was harder than I expected. I kept thinking about assignments that were due. On Tuesday, I made a list of my tasks before I left the classroom. Once I could see what I needed to do later, it was easier to relax during the break. Ana and I sat near the soccer field and talked about everything except schoolwork. I noticed that I returned to class with more energy.

The experiment didn’t make my homework shorter, so I had to be more organized in the evening. I still work through lunch sometimes, especially when a deadline is close. But now I know that I can do better work if I have had a proper pause. I also look forward to seeing Ana, which is a good reason to keep taking the break.

questions.prompt: What led the writer to rethink a habit that had seemed productive?
options: The writer wanted to test Ana’s routine.
The school stopped allowing lunch at desks.
Ana needed help with an evening task.
The writer had finished all homework.
questions.answer: The writer wanted to test Ana’s routine.
questions.explanation: Ana invited the writer to join, so the writer tried her method for a week.

questions.prompt: Why was writing a list useful even though it did not finish any of the work?
options: It gave the writer more homework to do.
It helped the writer stop worrying about what to do later.
It helped Ana choose a place to eat.
It meant that the writer could finish all work before lunch.
questions.answer: It helped the writer stop worrying about what to do later.
questions.explanation: Seeing the work written down made it easier to relax.

questions.prompt: What change suggested that the lunch experiment was helping during the school day?
options: It became much longer.
There were more assignments.
The writer felt more energetic.
Ana no longer joined.
questions.explanation: The writer returned with more energy.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported even though the experiment didn’t reduce the amount of homework?
options: Taking a break can improve the way you work.
The best time to study is always lunchtime.
Writing lists makes homework shorter.
Friends should always do homework together.
questions.answer: Taking a break can improve the way you work.
questions.explanation: The writer concludes that a proper pause can make later work better.

I signed up for the park project because I wanted to learn more about local birds. On the first day, the guide explained that the project also repaired paths after storms. [1] I decided to help with that work too.

My group was given a fairly long path to check. It seemed like a lot of work until the guide suggested a plan. [2] This meant that we could note the problems as we went, without missing any part of the trail.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Read the questions. Listen twice and choose one answer for each question.
parts.transcript:
Narrator: Question one. You hear two friends talking after lunch.
Maya: Is your headache any better, Sam?
Ben: A little. I thought it was because I hadn't eaten enough, but I had lunch and it didn't help. I feel better now that I've had some water.
Maya: You should take a bottle with you next time.

Narrator: Question two. You hear two people preparing a talk.
Ben: Why don't we practice the whole talk once more?
Maya: We know most of it. I'd rather spend the time fixing the last slide. It doesn't explain what the audience should do next.
Ben: You're right. Let's change the final message now.

Narrator: Question three. You hear two friends talking about a weekend outdoors.
Maya: Was the wildlife center busy?
Ben: Quite busy in the morning. Things were quieter after lunch, and a volunteer showed us how they help injured birds. That was more interesting than seeing the birds from a distance.
Maya: I'd like to go on a guided visit, too.

Narrator: Question four. You hear two friends discussing a new activity.
Ben: So, would you try kayaking again?
Maya: Probably, but only on a calm river. I liked being on the water, but I spent the whole time worrying because our boat was moving so fast. I'd choose an easier trip next time.

options: Eating lunch
Taking a nap
Drinking water
questions.explanation: Lunch did not help. He felt better after drinking water.

questions.explanation: They decide to clarify the final message.

parts.title: An interview about a challenge
parts.instructions: Read the questions. Listen twice and choose one answer for each question.
parts.transcript:
Narrator: You will hear an interview with a student who started a quiet lunch club.
Maya: Why did you start the lunch club, Nico?
Ben: I used to spend every break finishing homework. After a while I noticed I couldn't concentrate in the afternoon. I wanted a proper break and thought others might need one too.
Maya: Was the club popular at first?
Ben: Only three people came on the first day. The original room was right by the cafeteria and it was so noisy that we had to move. The library gave us a corner, and after that a lot more people joined.
Maya: Will you change anything next month?
Ben: Some people want us to add activities every day, but a long list of activities might make it feel like another lesson. I'd rather keep the club relaxed. We can offer games or books and let people choose.
